lessons.title: Preparing to cultivate a seed trial
lessons.html:
Preparing to cultivate a seed trial

Seed companies and research stations plant trials to compare new cultivars and breeding lines with known cultivars. A trial is only useful if every plot is treated the same way, apart from the cultivar. If one plot gets more water, fertiliser or weed control than another, the yield difference may have nothing to do with genetics. Cultivating a trial means looking after it from planting to harvest so that the comparison stays fair.

Know the trial

  • Read the trial protocol: aim of the trial, entries, layout, plot size, replications, planting date and the operations planned (fertiliser, weed control, irrigation, pest control).
  • Study the field plan. Each plot has a number, and plots of the same entry are spread over replications (blocks) at random.
  • Find the trial in the field: corner pegs, block markers and plot labels must match the plan.

Prepare people and equipment

  • Check that implements such as hand hoes, knapsack sprayers, small plot tractors and fertiliser spreaders are clean, calibrated and working.
  • Order inputs in time: fertiliser, registered herbicides and insecticides, irrigation schedule.
  • Brief the workers. Explain that trial plots are different from a commercial land: do not walk through plots, do not move labels, do not pull plants unless told.
  • Prepare data sheets or the tablet app for recording observations.

Safety

Where chemicals will be applied, only trained operators with the PPE on the label may spray. Check wind before spraying so drift does not damage neighbouring plots or other trials. Follow the label for re-entry before workers go into sprayed plots to take notes.

lessons.title: Growing the trial
lessons.html:
Growing the trial

During the season the aim is uniform management and accurate observation. Every operation must be done on the whole trial at the same time, preferably on the same day.

Crop care operations

  • Thinning: after emergence, thin plots to the target plant population in the protocol, so all entries start equal.
  • Gap filling: only where the protocol allows. Otherwise record the gaps.
  • Fertiliser: apply top-dressing evenly across all plots at the rate in the protocol.
  • Weed control: keep plots and paths clean, by hoeing or registered herbicides. Weedy plots give false low yields.
  • Irrigation: water the trial evenly. Check that sprinklers or drippers cover every plot.
  • Pest and disease control: scout regularly and act according to the protocol. In some trials, disease is not controlled on purpose because the aim is to compare tolerance. Check before spraying.

Observations

ObservationExample
Emergence and stand countPlants per plot at a set stage
Flowering dateDate 50% of plants show silks or tassels
Plant and ear heightMeasured on a set number of plants
Disease and pest scoresRated on the scale in the protocol
LodgingPlants fallen or broken
Off-typesPlants that do not match the entry

Write observations on the day, with plot number and date. Never fill in data later from memory. Note events that affect the trial: hail, flooding of a corner, animal damage or a sprayer fault.

lessons.title: Completing the cultivation process
lessons.html:
Completing the cultivation process

As the crop matures, the cultivation phase ends and the trial is prepared for harvest. This stage makes sure the data collected during the season is complete and that the trial can be harvested correctly.

Before harvest

  • Do final observations such as maturity date, final stand count and lodging.
  • Check all plot labels and markers. Replace damaged labels using the field plan, never from guesswork.
  • Trim plot ends or alleys if the protocol requires a set harvest length.
  • Protect the trial from birds, baboons, monkeys, porcupines or cattle where these are a risk, for example by fencing, bird scaring or extra checks.

Data checks

  1. Compare data sheets with the field plan. Every plot should have every observation.
  2. Look for unusual values, for example a plant height of 25 m instead of 2.5 m. Check them against field notes.
  3. Capture data into the trial database or spreadsheet and keep the original sheets.
  4. Report trial events that may affect results, such as uneven irrigation, to the trial manager.

Equipment and inputs

Clean and store hand tools and sprayers. Return unused chemicals to the locked store and record the quantity used. Triple rinse empty containers for approved disposal.

Communicating

Give the trial manager a short summary: condition of the trial, problems during the season, completeness of data and when it will be ready for harvest. A trial that has suffered badly from hail or flood may need to be dropped, and the manager must decide this.

Key points

  • A fair trial needs the same management on every plot.
  • Follow the protocol for thinning, fertiliser, weeds, water and pest control.
  • Record observations on the day with plot numbers.
  • Keep labels and markers matched to the field plan.
  • Check data for gaps and errors before harvest.

quiz.question: Why must every plot in a trial be managed the same way?

options.text: So differences come from the cultivar, not the management
It makes the field look neat

quiz.question: Where do you find the planned plant population and fertiliser rate?
A plot label is missing. How should it be replaced?

options.text: Copy the label from the next plot

quiz.question: When should observations be written down?

options.text: At the end of the season
On the day, with plot number and date

quiz.question: Why might a trial not be sprayed for a disease?

options.text: The trial may be comparing disease tolerance
Chemicals are never used on trials
